title: Can a robot nail wall sheathing to code tolerance, and what decides it?
lede: research programme on robotic sheathing of a wood-frame wall; milestone 1: APA's 1/8 in panel gap shrinks the joint-nail window from ±3.93 to ±3.14 mm and the stud reading needed for 95% clean sheets from 0.90 to 0.41 mm, a sheet must hang plumb to about 0.03° even when the robot aims from the measured edge, and sheets butted along a wall leave their studs by the third (full panels) or fifth (1/16 in trimmed) sheet, while setting each from its own studs keeps 98% clean
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) asking whether a stock humanoid, a mobile manipulator with a lift or a purpose-built gantry can hang a 4x8 sheet of wall sheathing and land all 62 nails where the panel maker and the code want them, which error source decides it, and what a clean sheet costs; it gathers track 20's 26 buildbot-* projects into one question aimed at Automation in Construction. Milestone 1 adds what earlier projects left out: panels are hung with a 1/8 in gap (APA's recommendation) centred on the joint stud, sheets are hung slightly off and out of plumb, and their width differs from the 48 in stud module. With the gap, the 34 joint nails' window shrinks from ±3.93 to ±3.14 mm, and the single stud reading needed for 95% clean sheets (0.9 mm tool scatter) falls from 0.90 to 0.41 mm; at buildbot-studfind's 0.89 mm only 75% of sheets come out clean, 56% if the robot does not plan for the gap. With a 0.5 mm stud reading, a robot aiming at the design window has no tolerance for sheet pose at all; aiming from the measured sheet edge (to 0.5 mm) allows 0.44 mm of translation and 0.031° of rotation (1σ), and halves the weight of the stud error. Along a 40 ft wall, sheets butted with a 1/8 in gauge drift 3.2 mm a sheet: no third sheet is clean with full panels, and panels trimmed 1/16 in keep a joint window for four sheets; setting each sheet from its own studs keeps every sheet at 98% clean. Monte Carlo checked against buildbot-studfind and closed forms. Stud, edge, gauge and width errors are swept, not measured; the gap, edge distance and trim come from APA pages seen in search results; studs are straight and nothing is tested on hardware.
